Paul suggests that God may have allowed this painful separation for a good end. Scripture shows God working this way elsewhere. Joseph's brothers sold him into slavery, and years later Joseph told them, "But as for you, you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good, in order to bring it about as it is this day, to save many people alive" (Genesis 50:20). That did not make the brothers' sin acceptable, and God's providence would still leave room for dealing with any wrong or debt (v. 18). Paul invites Philemon to look beyond the separation and to consider what God may have been doing through it all. Onesimus left as an unbeliever and was coming back as a believer.

"that you might receive him forever,"

The Greek verb translated "receive" means to have something in full. It was used in business for a receipt marked "paid in full," and Jesus used it when He said the hypocrites "have their reward" (Matthew 6:2). Philemon lost Onesimus for a short time, but he was getting him back completely.

The contrast between "for a while" and "forever" is the heart of the verse. The word "forever" is the word usually translated "eternal" or "everlasting." Before, Philemon had Onesimus only as a slave, a relationship that would end at death at the latest. Now that both men belong to Christ, they share a bond that will never end. A brief separation had led to a relationship that will last into eternity.
15.notes: The letter describes Onesimus’s absence as a departure for a time (v. 15) and leaves the circumstances of his meeting with Paul open. Paul’s “perhaps” concerns what God may have brought about through the separation.

reflections.title: Providence Beneath the Rebellion
reflections.html: “For perhaps he departed for a while for this purpose, that you might receive him forever.” Paul looks at Onesimus’s flight, and whatever wrong came with it, through the lens of God’s overarching providence. His “perhaps” is humble; he does not claim to know God’s purposes fully. Yet he dares to suggest that God was quietly at work beneath the rebellion. God did not author the sin, but He overruled it, steering the runaway into the path of the apostle and turning a temporary loss into an eternal gain. What looked like a relational rupture became the doorway to a forever brotherhood. God is able to take human failure, sin, and departure and weave them into a larger tapestry of reconciliation.
reflections.q: “For perhaps he departed for a while for this purpose, that you might receive him forever.”

16.brief: Here is the heart of the letter: Philemon is to have Onesimus back “no longer as a slave but more than a slave,” as “a beloved brother.” Onesimus is especially dear to Paul, but “how much more” to Philemon, “both in the flesh and in the Lord,” so their new brotherhood must be lived out in the everyday relationship of their household as well as in their shared faith.
16.explain:
"no longer as a slave but more than a slave—"

Onesimus had run away from Philemon's household as a slave, and now Paul was sending him back. Under Roman law a slave was legally his master's property, and a runaway could expect harsh treatment. Paul asks Philemon to see Onesimus differently. The word "as" matters. Paul does not say here that Onesimus has stopped being a slave. He says Philemon should no longer think of him or treat him as only a slave. Whatever his legal position, that is no longer the most important thing about him. Onesimus has become something "more."

Elsewhere Paul taught that in Christ "there is neither slave nor free" and that "you are all one in Christ Jesus" (Galatians 3:28). A believing slave is "the Lord's freedman," and a free believer is "Christ's slave" (1 Corinthians 7:22). Philemon and Onesimus now stand on the same ground before God, and that changes how a Christian master must treat a Christian slave.

"a beloved brother,"

This is what Onesimus has become. "Brother" means a fellow believer, a member of God's family with the same heavenly Father. A slave was usually treated as someone outside the family, even when he lived in the household. Now Onesimus belongs to the same family as his master.

Paul also calls him "beloved." He had used that word for Philemon, "our beloved friend" (v. 1), and for Apphia, "the beloved Apphia" (v. 2). Now the runaway slave receives the same title as the head of the house. Paul describes Onesimus the same way to the church at Colossae, calling him "a faithful and beloved brother, who is one of you" (Colossians 4:9). The young man who left as a runaway was coming back as a dearly loved member of the church that met in Philemon's own home.

"especially to me but how much more to you,"

Onesimus was especially dear to Paul, who had led him to faith in prison and called him his son (v. 10). Yet Paul says he should mean even more to Philemon. Paul would soon be separated from Onesimus by distance. Philemon would live with him, work beside him, and worship with him. The brotherhood Paul enjoyed for a short time in prison, Philemon could enjoy every day.

"both in the flesh and in the Lord."

"In the flesh" refers to Philemon's earthly connection with Onesimus: their life together in the same household, with its daily work and ordinary dealings as master and servant. "In the Lord" refers to their new spiritual bond as two men who both belong to Christ. Paul's tie to Onesimus was only spiritual, but Philemon's was both. This means their brotherhood in Christ could not stay limited to Sunday worship. It had to shape how Philemon spoke to Onesimus, how he treated him, and how he directed his work. Paul told Christian masters to give their servants "what is just and fair, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven" (Colossians 4:1). For Philemon, receiving Onesimus as a beloved brother would mean welcoming him back into his home on new terms, in everyday life as well as in the Lord.
16.notes:
Slavery in the Roman world was not based on race. People became slaves through war, debt, birth, or kidnapping, and freeing slaves was common, especially in cities.

It was still a system in which a human being was legal property and could be beaten or sold.

reflections.title: No Longer a Slave, but a Beloved Brother
reflections.html: “No longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother.” Paul does not directly attack the institution of Roman slavery here; instead he places something beneath it that it cannot survive. If Philemon receives Onesimus as a beloved brother, the master-slave relationship is changed at its root. The cross levels the ground and turns property into family. Paul does not explicitly say that Onesimus must be freed, but he asks for something no legal arrangement could hold: brotherhood “both in the flesh and in the Lord.”
reflections.q: “No longer as a slave but more than a slave, a beloved brother.”

17.brief: Now Paul states the request plainly: “If then you count me as a partner, receive him as you would me.” Because Philemon shares a common life in Christ with Paul, he is to welcome Onesimus on the strength of Paul’s standing, with the same warmth he would give Paul himself.
17.explain:
"If then you count me as a partner,"

"Then" ties this request to what Paul has just said: Onesimus is coming back "no longer as a slave but more than a slave—a beloved brother" (1:16). Because that is who Onesimus now is, Paul makes his request. The "if" does not express doubt. Paul is not wondering whether Philemon values him. He is calling on a partnership both men already know is real.

The Greek word for "partner" describes someone who shares a common life, work, or stake with another. Luke uses it for James and John, "who were partners with Simon" in the fishing business (Luke 5:10). Partners hold things in common, so what concerns one concerns the other. Paul has already called Philemon a "fellow laborer" (1:1), and the word is closely related to the one translated "sharing" in Paul's prayer that "the sharing of your faith may become effective" (1:6). Here that prayer becomes concrete. Philemon's partnership with Paul in the gospel is not only a warm feeling or a shared history of ministry. It will show itself in how he treats the person standing at his door.

"receive him as you would me."

The word "receive" means to welcome someone into your home and your company. It is the same verb Paul uses in Romans 15:7: "Therefore receive one another, just as Christ also received us, to the glory of God." Think about how Philemon would welcome Paul if he arrived at Colossae: with joy, a place at the table, and the best room in the house. Paul even asks him to "prepare a guest room for me" (1:22). That is the welcome Paul asks him to give Onesimus. A runaway slave would normally come back expecting anger and punishment. Paul asks that he be greeted like an honored friend.

Paul has already called Onesimus "my own heart" (1:12). Now he goes further and asks Philemon to treat Onesimus as Paul himself. Paul binds himself so closely to Onesimus that whatever Philemon does to one, he does to the other. Jesus spoke the same way about His messengers: "He who receives you receives Me" (Matthew 10:40).

This gives a meaningful picture of how God receives those who trust in Christ. Onesimus had no standing of his own to bring back to Philemon. He came carrying Paul's name and Paul's welcome. In the same way, sinners have no standing of their own before God, but those who belong to Christ are received because of their union with Him. Paul says God "made us accepted in the Beloved" (Ephesians 1:6). Not every detail of Paul, Philemon, and Onesimus matches God's dealings with us, but the heart of the picture is clear: a person is welcomed because of his connection to someone who is already loved and accepted.

reflections.title: Receive Him as You Would Me
reflections.html: “If then you count me as a partner, receive him as you would me.” Paul asks Philemon to treat a guilty runaway as if he were the apostle himself. Here is one of the clearest pictures of our acceptance before God in all the New Testament. Christ does not merely ask that we be tolerated; He brings us to the Father in His own name, and we are “accepted in the Beloved” (Ephesians 1:6). The picture is not a perfect parallel, since Philemon is no sinless judge and Paul is no divine Savior, but it shows the shape of the gospel unmistakably: the guilty one is received on the standing of another.
reflections.q: “If then you count me as a partner, receive him as you would me.”

18.brief: Paul adds, “But if he has wronged you or owes anything, put that on my account.” Without naming any wrong or debt, Paul offers to have whatever may stand against Onesimus charged to himself, a clear picture of Christ, who bore our sin so that we could be reconciled to God, though only Christ’s sacrifice actually atones for sin.
18.explain:
"But if he has wronged you or owes anything,"

Paul speaks of two possibilities: Onesimus may have wronged Philemon or may owe him something. The first concerns harm or injustice, and the second concerns an obligation to repay. The verse leaves both possibilities open.

The word “if” matters. Paul leaves the facts of any claim open and offers to bear the cost himself. His offer is part of a personal appeal that the congregation will hear.

"put that on my account."

This is the language of business records. The Greek verb means to charge something to someone's account, the way a merchant writes a debt under a customer's name. Paul asks Philemon to charge him for whatever Onesimus may owe. He makes the promise in his own hand in the next verse. Paul offers to take away any such obstacle so that nothing would stand in the way of Philemon receiving Onesimus as a brother.

Paul’s offer gives a picture of Christ’s work. We stood before God guilty, with a debt of sin we could never repay. Christ bore our sins and brought us to God. “For Christ also suffered once for sins, the just for the unjust, that He might bring us to God” (1 Peter 3:18). Paul offers to meet whatever claim Philemon may have. Christ actually bore our sins and paid the cost with His life.

reflections.title: Put That on My Account
reflections.html: “But if he has wronged you or owes anything, put that on my account.” The verb means to charge it to someone’s account. Paul does not specify the wrong; the traditional understanding is that Onesimus had cost Philemon something, perhaps through theft or simply through lost labor. Whatever it was, Paul steps into the gap for a guilty runaway and offers to absorb the debt himself. In one phrase he becomes a living picture of the gospel: Jesus Christ took the debt of our sin onto His own account so that we could be received. Paul offered to pay money; Christ paid with His blood. The picture points beyond itself to a substitution far greater than Paul’s.
reflections.q: “But if he has wronged you or owes anything, put that on my account.”

19.brief: Taking the pen himself, Paul writes, “I, Paul, am writing with my own hand. I will repay,” a signed promise Philemon could hold him to. He then adds a pointed reminder that “you owe me even your own self besides,” most likely because Philemon came to faith through Paul’s ministry, so any debt Onesimus may owe is small beside what Philemon has received.
19.explain:
"I, Paul, am writing with my own hand."

Paul usually dictated his letters to a helper who wrote them down. One of them, Tertius, even added his own greeting in Romans (Romans 16:22). Paul would often take the pen at the end to add a greeting in his own handwriting as a mark that the letter was genuinely his (2 Thessalonians 3:17). Here his handwriting does more than confirm who wrote the letter. In the ancient world, a statement of debt written in a person's own hand was a binding promise to pay, much like a signed IOU today. By writing these words himself, Paul turns the offer he just made, "put that on my account" (v. 18), into a commitment Philemon could hold him to.

"I will repay—"

The Greek word for "repay" was used for paying damages or making good on a loss. Paul does not simply ask Philemon to overlook a possible loss. Paul offers to cover whatever loss Philemon may have suffered so that nothing stands in the way of Philemon receiving him.

Paul’s handwritten pledge illustrates Christ’s costly work of reconciliation. Paul stood ready to cover any wrong or debt so that Onesimus could be welcomed. Christ gave His own life to bring guilty people to God (1 Peter 3:18).

"not to mention to you that you owe me even your own self besides."

Paul says he will "not mention" something, and then mentions it, a gentle way of reminding Philemon of something they both knew. Most likely Philemon came to faith through Paul's ministry, perhaps during Paul's long stay in Ephesus, when "all who dwelt in Asia heard the word of the Lord Jesus" (Acts 19:10). Paul had never visited Colossae himself (Colossians 2:1), so Philemon probably met him elsewhere. If Philemon heard the gospel from Paul, then he owed Paul far more than money. He owed him the message through which he received eternal life.

Paul places any amount Onesimus may owe beside what Philemon has received through Paul’s ministry. His written promise remains in force. The reminder gives Philemon a reason to act generously. Jesus’ parable of the unforgiving servant makes a related point about extending the mercy one has received (Matthew 18:21–35).

reflections.title: An IOU in His Own Hand
reflections.html: “I, Paul, am writing with my own hand. I will repay, not to mention to you that you owe me even your own self besides.” Paul signs a formal promise to pay, in his own handwriting, to make it binding. Then, with gentle pastoral irony, he reminds Philemon that he owes Paul his very self, since Paul had led him to Christ. When others wrong us, we stay humble by remembering the infinite, unpayable debt of grace we owe to God, and our debt to those who brought that grace to us.
reflections.q: “I, Paul, am writing with my own hand.

20.brief: Calling him “brother” again, Paul asks, “let me have joy from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in the Lord.” Philemon has refreshed the hearts of the saints (v. 7), and Paul now asks him to refresh his own heart in the same way, by welcoming the one Paul has called “my own heart.”
20.explain:
"Yes, brother,"

"Yes" carries Paul's appeal to its final, warm request. He has just offered to repay whatever Onesimus owes and gently reminded Philemon that he owes Paul "even your own self besides" (1:19). Now he speaks as family. "Brother" marks Philemon as a fellow believer, and it is the same word Paul used when he praised the way Philemon had refreshed God's people (1:7). Paul is not pulling rank. He is speaking to a brother he loves about a brother they now share.

"let me have joy from you in the Lord;"

The Greek verb behind "let me have joy" means to receive benefit or delight from someone. It comes from the same root as the name Onesimus, which means "useful" or "profitable." Paul seems to be gently playing on the name again. He is asking Philemon to let him enjoy the benefit of this request: in receiving the useful one, Philemon will be useful to Paul. After mentioning the debt Philemon owes him, Paul asks for repayment in only one form, the joy of seeing Onesimus welcomed.

"In the Lord" shows what kind of joy Paul wants. He is not asking a personal favor for his own comfort. He is asking for the joy that comes when believers who belong to Christ treat one another as Christ would have them do.

"refresh my heart in the Lord."

This request repeats the words Paul used to praise Philemon earlier: "the hearts of the saints have been refreshed by you, brother" (1:7). The word "refresh" means to give rest or relief, like a weary traveler finally able to stop and recover. Philemon was known for bringing that kind of relief to other believers. Now Paul, sitting in chains for Christ, asks Philemon to do for him what he has already done for so many others.

The word "heart" here refers to the inner self, the place of deepest affection, and Paul has already used it for Onesimus. When he sent him back, he called him "my own heart" (1:12). Since Onesimus is so closely bound to Paul's affections, Philemon cannot refresh Paul's heart while turning Onesimus away. The way to give Paul rest is to receive Onesimus kindly. Philemon's welcome to his returning slave would reach all the way to a prison cell and lift the spirit of the apostle who loved them both.

reflections.title: Refresh the Heart of Your Leader
reflections.html: “Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in the Lord.” Leaders are usually the ones pouring themselves out to refresh others, as Philemon had done for the saints (v. 7). Here Paul admits his own need. Believers can deeply refresh the hearts of their pastors and leaders through bold acts of obedience and love. (“Let me have joy,” or “benefit,” may itself be a quiet play on the name Onesimus, “profitable.”)
reflections.q: “Yes, brother, let me have joy from you in the Lord; refresh my heart in the Lord.”

21.brief: Paul writes “having confidence in your obedience,” a word that shows his appeal still carries apostolic weight, yet he expects more than bare compliance: Philemon “will do even more than I say.” Paul may be hinting that Onesimus could be freed or sent back to help him (compare v. 13), but the letter leaves that “more” unnamed.
21.explain:
"Having confidence in your obedience, I write to you,"

Paul has spent this letter appealing rather than commanding. He said he could have been "very bold in Christ to command you what is fitting, yet for love's sake I rather appeal to you" (vv. 8–9), and he refused to keep Onesimus without Philemon's consent, so that his good deed would not be "by compulsion, as it were, but voluntary" (v. 14). Now, near the end, Paul uses the word "obedience." He is not quietly taking back his gentle tone. The obedience he has in mind is a willing response to what is right in the Lord. Paul had set aside his authority as an apostle, but what he asked still carried real moral weight, and he trusted Philemon to recognize it and act on it.

Paul's confidence was not flattery. He had heard of Philemon's "love and faith which you have toward the Lord Jesus and toward all the saints" (v. 5), and he knew Philemon had refreshed the hearts of God's people (v. 7). A man with that kind of record could be trusted to do what love required. By putting his confidence in writing, Paul also let Philemon know what he expected. The whole church meeting in his house would hear the letter, so his response would be seen by fellow believers who knew what Paul had asked.

"knowing that you will do even more than I say."

Paul has asked Philemon to receive Onesimus as he would receive Paul himself (v. 17) and to charge any wrong Onesimus may have done to Paul's account (v. 18). Now Paul says he expects Philemon to go beyond even that. He does not explain what "more" means. Many interpreters think Paul was hoping Philemon would set Onesimus free, especially since Paul had already asked him to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave but more than a slave—a beloved brother" (v. 16). Others suggest Paul hoped Philemon would send Onesimus back to help him, since Paul had wanted to keep him for service during his imprisonment (v. 13). Either is possible, but Paul does not say which he meant.

By leaving the "more" unnamed, Paul stays consistent with the rest of the letter. He has already given up commanding, so he does not now spell out a further demand. He leaves room for Philemon to decide for himself how far his love will go. Paul's confidence rests on the kind of man Philemon already was: someone who would not settle for the bare minimum when a brother in Christ was involved.

reflections.title: Grace Does Even More
reflections.html: “Having confidence in your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.” The law sets a minimum; grace overflows the boundaries of duty. Paul expects not bare compliance but generous, above-and-beyond love. What that “more” was, Scripture does not say. It may suggest Paul’s hope that Onesimus would be set free, or allowed to return and help Paul in the work of the gospel. The text leaves the door open, and grace is the kind of thing that walks through open doors.
reflections.q: “Having confidence in your obedience, I write to you, knowing that you will do even more than I say.”

22.brief: Meanwhile Paul asks Philemon to “prepare a guest room for me,” trusting that “through your prayers” he will be “granted to you.” In Greek this “your” is plural, so Paul is counting on the whole church to pray for his release, and a visit would let him see for himself how Onesimus has been received.
22.explain:
"But, meanwhile, also prepare a guest room for me,"

Paul has finished his appeal for Onesimus, and now he adds a personal request. "Meanwhile" means at the same time: while Philemon acts on what Paul has asked, he should also get a room ready for Paul. The Greek word for "guest room" means lodging or hospitality, a place to stay as a guest. Early Christians were expected to welcome traveling believers into their homes (Romans 12:13), and Philemon already opened his house to the church and had "refreshed" the hearts of God's people (v. 7). Paul could ask this of him as easily as one friend asks another.

The request also carries a gentle weight. If Paul came to visit, he would see for himself how Philemon had welcomed Onesimus. He does not say this as a threat. He has already said he is confident Philemon will do even more than he asks (v. 21). But the prospect of seeing Paul face to face would give Philemon every reason to follow through gladly.

"for I trust that through your prayers I shall be granted to you."

"I trust" translates a Greek word meaning "I hope." Paul expected to be released from his chains for Christ, but he did not claim to know it for certain. He spoke the same way in Philippians: "I trust in the Lord that I myself shall also come shortly" (Philippians 2:24). Scripture does not tell us whether Paul ever made this visit to Philemon.

In Greek, both "your" and "you" are plural here, even though the command to prepare a room is spoken to Philemon alone. Paul is counting on the prayers of the whole church in Philemon's house. Early in the letter he told Philemon that he remembered him in his own prayers (v. 4). Now he asks the church to pray for him. Paul believed God works through His people's prayers. He wrote to the Philippians that his situation would "turn out for my deliverance through your prayer and the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ" (Philippians 1:19).

The word "granted" means given freely as a gift, and it comes from the same root as "grace," God's undeserved kindness. If Paul was released, it would not be because Rome owed him freedom. It would be God's gift, given to the church in answer to their prayers. The believers would receive Paul back as a gift from God, much as Philemon was being asked to receive Onesimus back.

reflections.title: Make the Bed: Expectant Prayer
reflections.html: “But meanwhile also prepare a guest room for me, for I trust that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.” Paul joins God’s sovereignty, his release from a Roman prison, with the intercession of the church. He is so confident in their prayers that he tells them to get the room ready. Faith prays, and then makes the bed.
reflections.q: “But meanwhile also prepare a guest room for me, for I trust that through your prayers I shall be granted to you.”

23.brief: Epaphras, whom Paul calls “my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus,” sends his greetings to Philemon. Colossians 4:12 calls Epaphras “one of you,” so he most likely came from Philemon’s own community, and Paul honors him as one who shares his captivity for Christ’s sake.
23.explain:
"Epaphras,"

Epaphras was a Colossian, "one of you," as Paul told that church (Colossians 4:12). He seems to have been the one who first brought the gospel to Colossae, since Paul reminded the believers there that they had heard the truth "as you also learned from Epaphras, our dear fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on your behalf" (Colossians 1:7). He also cared for the believers in the nearby towns of Laodicea and Hierapolis (Colossians 4:13). Even while away from home, he kept "laboring fervently for you in prayers, that you may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God" (Colossians 4:12). Philemon and the church in his house would have known Epaphras well, and some of them likely first heard about Jesus from him.

"my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus,"

The Greek word for "fellow prisoner" literally describes a fellow captive, someone taken prisoner in war. Paul uses the same word for Aristarchus (Colossians 4:10) and for Andronicus and Junia (Romans 16:7). Scripture does not say whether Epaphras had been arrested himself or had chosen to share Paul's confinement so he could stay with him. Either way, he was suffering alongside Paul for the same reason. Paul calls himself "a prisoner of Christ Jesus" (v. 1), and Epaphras shared those chains "in Christ Jesus," because he belonged to Christ and served Him. The picture of a fellow captive also fits the soldier language Paul used for Archippus, "our fellow soldier" (v. 2). These men were in the same fight, and partnership in the gospel cost them more than effort. It cost them their freedom.

"greets you,"

The "you" here is singular in Greek, so Epaphras sends his greeting to Philemon personally. Many interpreters see more than courtesy in it. Epaphras was a respected teacher from Philemon's own church, and his greeting comes at the end of a letter asking Philemon to welcome back Onesimus, his runaway slave, as a brother. When Philemon heard the letter read, he would know that Epaphras stood with Paul, and that this man he trusted shared Paul's love for the new believer now returning home.

reflections.title: The Fellowship of Suffering
reflections.html: “Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you.” Epaphras had brought the gospel to Colossae, the town where Philemon’s house church met (Colossians 1:7; 4:12). Now he shares Paul’s confinement. Shared suffering for the gospel forges a deep and unbreakable bond.
reflections.q: “Epaphras, my fellow prisoner in Christ Jesus, greets you.”

24.brief: Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, and Luke also send greetings, and Paul calls them “my fellow laborers.” Philemon, whom Paul named a “fellow laborer” in verse 1, is reminded that he belongs to a wider company of workers in the gospel who stand with Paul.
24.explain:
"as do Mark,"

These men join Epaphras in sending greetings to Philemon (v. 23). The same group sends greetings at the end of Colossians (Colossians 4:10–14), the letter that went to the same town with Onesimus on the same journey (Colossians 4:9).

Mark is John Mark, "the cousin of Barnabas" (Colossians 4:10). Years earlier he had abandoned Paul and Barnabas partway through their first missionary journey (Acts 13:13). When Barnabas later wanted to take him along again, Paul refused, and the disagreement was so sharp that the two men parted ways (Acts 15:37–39). Now Mark is back at Paul's side in prison, and Paul had already told the Colossians to welcome him if he came (Colossians 4:10). Near the end of his life Paul wrote, "Get Mark and bring him with you, for he is useful to me for ministry" (2 Timothy 4:11). The Greek word for "useful" there is the same word Paul uses for Onesimus, who "once was unprofitable to you, but now is profitable to you and to me" (v. 11). Philemon was being asked to welcome back the man who had run away from his household, and Mark himself showed that such a person could become a valued servant of Christ.

"Aristarchus,"

Aristarchus came from Thessalonica in Macedonia (Acts 20:4; 27:2). He was with Paul in Ephesus when a mob dragged him into the theater during the riot over the goddess Diana (Acts 19:29), and he sailed with Paul on the dangerous voyage to Rome (Acts 27:2). In Colossians Paul calls him "my fellow prisoner" (Colossians 4:10). He had stayed with Paul through mobs, shipwreck, and chains.

"Demas,"

Demas is also named among those greeting the Colossians (Colossians 4:14), and here he is counted as one of Paul's fellow laborers. Sadly, his story did not end well. Paul later wrote, "Demas has forsaken me, having loved this present world, and has departed for Thessalonica" (2 Timothy 4:10). Mark had once turned back and later proved faithful. Demas served faithfully for a time and later turned away.

"Luke,"

Paul calls him "the beloved physician" (Colossians 4:14). Luke wrote the Gospel that bears his name and the book of Acts, and in Acts he often says "we" when describing Paul's travels, showing that he was there himself, including the voyage to Rome (Acts 27:1). He stayed with Paul to the end. In his final imprisonment Paul wrote, "Only Luke is with me" (2 Timothy 4:11).

"my fellow laborers."

Paul does not describe these men as his assistants or followers but as workers alongside him in the gospel. He used the same title for Philemon in the opening of the letter (v. 1). Philemon was being asked to act as a member of this same team, and Onesimus, now a believer, was joining that company as well.

reflections.title: Mark Restored, Demas Departing
reflections.html: “As do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my fellow workers.” Years earlier Mark had left Paul in the middle of a missionary journey (Acts 13:13), and Paul thought him unfit to take again, a disagreement sharp enough to divide Paul and Barnabas (Acts 15:37–39). Now Mark stands beside Paul as a fellow worker, restored. Later Paul would write that Mark was “useful to me for ministry” (2 Timothy 4:11), the very word he used of Onesimus here. How fitting that a restored deserter is present when Paul writes asking forgiveness for a runaway. Demas, by contrast, is listed here as a fellow worker, yet a few years later he abandoned Paul, “having loved this present world” (2 Timothy 4:10). One man who failed was restored; one man who served would fall away. Past failure does not guarantee future uselessness, and past faithfulness does not guarantee future endurance.
reflections.q: “As do Mark, Aristarchus, Demas, Luke, my fellow workers.”

25.brief: Paul ends with a blessing: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.” In Greek this “your” is plural, so the grace that opened the letter (v. 3) now rests on the whole church, and that same grace makes possible the welcome Paul has asked for.
25.explain:
"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ"

Paul opened the letter with "Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ" (v. 3), and now he closes it the same way. Grace is God's undeserved kindness, His favor given to people who have not earned it and could never repay it. Everything Paul asked of Philemon lies between these two mentions of grace. Paul asked him to forgive, to welcome back the man who had run away, and to treat that man as a beloved brother. That request makes sense only among people who have already received grace themselves. Philemon had been forgiven a debt he could never pay, and Christ bore the cost of his sin so that he could be reconciled to God. Now Paul prays for that same grace to stay with him as he decides how to receive Onesimus.

The word "our" matters here. Paul, Timothy, Philemon, Apphia, Archippus, the church in Philemon's house, and now Onesimus all share one Lord. Philemon was Onesimus's earthly master, but both of them answered to the same Master. In the letter to the Colossians, likely written about the same time, Paul told masters to treat their servants justly, "knowing that you also have a Master in heaven" (Colossians 4:1). The grace Philemon depends on comes from the Lord who rules over him as well as over Onesimus.

"be with your spirit."

In Greek, "your" is plural here. Paul has addressed Philemon personally through most of the letter, but this closing blessing includes the whole church that would hear it read. The "spirit" is a person's inner life, the part of a person where God meets, strengthens, and changes them. Paul prays that Christ's grace will be at work deep inside each of them, not just shaping their outward behavior. Paul ends his letter to the Galatians with the same blessing: "Brethren, the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen" (Galatians 6:18).

"Amen."

"Amen" is a Hebrew word meaning "so be it" or "truly." It confirms the prayer as something Paul wholeheartedly wants and trusts God to do. When the letter was read aloud in Philemon's house, the believers gathered there could add their own "Amen" and join Paul in asking for that grace.

reflections.title: Grace for the Spirit
reflections.html: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit. Amen.” The letter begins with grace (v. 3) and ends with grace. Paul directs this grace to the spirit, the core of the person, because the radical forgiveness and relational change he has asked of Philemon cannot be produced by human willpower. It needs the sustained grace of Jesus Christ working at the deepest level of the heart. (“Your” is plural: the whole church in the house will need that grace to welcome Onesimus as family.)
reflections.q: “The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit.
